title: Noah
description: Biblical prophet known for building an ark
wiki_lead:
Noah (; Hebrew: נֹחַ, romanized: Nōaḥ, lit. 'rest' or 'consolation'; also Noach) appears as the last of the Antediluvian patriarchs in the traditions of Abrahamic religions. His story appears in the Hebrew Bible (Book of Genesis, chapters 5–9), the Quran and Baha'i writings, and extracanonically.
The Genesis flood narrative is among the best-known stories of the Bible. In this account, God decides to punish the evil ones. Noah then labors faithfully to build the Ark at God's command, ultimately saving not only his own family, but humankind itself and all land animals from extinction during the Flood. Afterwards, God makes a covenant with Noah and promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood. Noah is also portrayed as a "tiller of the soil" who is the first to cultivate the vine. After the flood, God commands Noah and his sons to "be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth."
The story of Noah in the Pentateuch is similar to the flood narrative in the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh, composed around 1800 BC, where a hero builds an ark to survive a divinely sent flood. Most scholars suggest that the biblical account was influenced by earlier Mesopotamian traditions, with notable parallels in plot elements and structure. Comparisons are also drawn between Noah and the Greek hero Deucalion, who, like Noah, is warned of a flood, builds an ark, and sends a bird to check on the flood's aftermath.

Biblical narrative


Noah's background
According to the genealogical account in Genesis 5, Noah, the son of Lamech, is the tenth and final antediluvian (pre-flood) patriarch. Lamech is 182 years old when Noah is born, and Noah is 500 years old when his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth are born. Lamech anticipated that Noah would "bring relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands".


Genesis flood narrative

The Genesis flood narrative is encompassed within chapters 6–9 in the Book of Genesis, in the Bible. The narrative indicates that God intended to return the Earth to its pre-Creation state of watery chaos by flooding the Earth because of humanity's misdeeds and then remake it using the microcosm of Noah's Ark. Thus, the flood was no ordinary overflow but a reversal of Creation. The narrative discusses the evil of humankind that moved God to destroy the world by way of the flood, the preparation of the ark for certain animals, Noah, and his family, and God's guarantee (the Noahic Covenant) for the continued existence of life under the promise that he would never send another flood.


After the flood

After the flood, Noah offered burnt offerings to God. God accepted the sacrifice, and made a covenant with Noah, and through him with all humankind, that he would not waste the earth or destroy man by another deluge.
"And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth". As a pledge of this gracious covenant with man and beast the rainbow was set in the clouds (ib. viii. 15–22, ix. 8–17). Injunctions were laid upon Noah: eating of animal food was permitted but not of living animals and the shedding of the blood of man by man was made a crime punishable by death at the hands of man (ib. ix. 3–6).


The Seven Laws of Noah

Furthermore we have The Seven Laws of Noah (citations to sources are there) as traditionally enumerated in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 56a-b) and Tosefta (Avodah Zarah 9:4), which are the following:

Not to worship idols.
Not to curse God.
Not to commit murder.
Not to commit adultery or sexual immorality.
Not to steal.
Not to eat flesh torn from a living animal.
To establish courts of justice.
Noah, as the last of the extremely long-lived Antediluvian patriarchs, died 350 years after the flood, at the age of 950, when Terah was 128. The maximum human lifespan, as depicted by the Bible, gradually diminishes thereafter, from almost 1,000 years to the 120 years of Moses.

grok_lead: Noah (Hebrew: × Ö¹×Ö·, Noaá¸¥) is a patriarch in the Abrahamic traditions, portrayed in the Book of Genesis as a righteous man selected by God to preserve humanity and animal life from a divine flood intended to eradicate widespread corruption on earth. According to the narrative, Noah, at 500 years old, fathered three sonsâShem, Ham, and Japhethâand later, at God's command, constructed a massive wooden ark to shelter his family and pairs of terrestrial creatures during the deluge that submerged the world for 150 days. The story culminates in Noah's release of a dove to confirm receding waters, the ark's resting on the mountains of Ararat, and God's covenant with him symbolized by the rainbow, promising never again to destroy the earth by flood. The Genesis account exhibits structural and thematic parallels to antecedent Mesopotamian flood myths, including the Sumerian Eridu Genesis, the Akkadian Atrahasis epic, and the Epic of Gilgamesh, where a favored human (such as Utnapishtim or Ziusudra) survives a god-sent inundation via a divinely instructed vessel, suggesting the biblical version adapted or polemized against these older Near Eastern traditions. Archaeological investigations reveal evidence of severe local floods in ancient Mesopotamia, such as sediment layers at sites like Ur and Shuruppak dating to around 2900 BCE, which may have inspired these shared cultural memories, though no geological or genetic data supports a singular global cataclysm capable of wiping out all terrestrial life except via the ark. As the purported ancestor of all post-flood humanity through his sons, Noah holds theological significance across Judaism, Christianity, and Islam (where he is known as Nuh), embodying themes of obedience, judgment, and renewal, while post-flood episodes like his vineyard planting and the cursing of Canaan via Ham's transgression have fueled historical interpretations and debates over lineage and morality. Despite affirmations of historicity in religious texts, secular scholarship, informed by stratigraphic continuity in civilizations like Egypt and China predating and postdating the purported era, regards the figure and event as legendary rather than empirically verifiable, with creationist claims of worldwide marine fossils and rapid sedimentation countered by uniformitarian models attributing such features to localized or gradual processes.
